items.title: Perimeter and area
items.content: Perimeter measures boundary length; area measures surface. Rectangle: \(P=2(l+b), A=lb\). Square: \(P=4s, A=s^2\). Triangle: \(A=\frac12 bh\). Parallelogram: \(A=bh\). Trapezium: \(A=\frac12(a+b)h\), where \(a,b\) are parallel sides. Circle: \(C=2\pi r=\pi d, A=\pi r^2\).

items.title: Units and composite figures
items.content: Perimeter uses linear units; area uses square units. Split a composite shape into familiar pieces, or subtract a cut-out. Convert all lengths to one unit before calculating.

items.title: Exam checks
items.content:
Convert lengths before using area formulas; 1 m² = 10,000 cm².
For circular calculations, state whether you used \(\pi=22/7\) or 3.14.

items.title: Rhombus, kite and sector formulas
items.content: Rhombus or kite area: (A= rac12d_1d_2), using perpendicular diagonals. Semicircle area: ( rac12pi r^2). Sector area for central angle (	heta) in degrees: ( rac{	heta}{360}pi r^2).

items.title: Rectangle and square
items.content: Worked example: a rectangle is 12 cm by 7 cm. \(P=2(12+7)=38\) cm and \(A=12\times7=84\) cm². A square of side 7 cm has perimeter 28 cm and area 49 cm².

items.title: Triangle and parallelogram
items.content: Triangle area uses perpendicular height, not a sloping side. Worked example: base 10 cm, height 6 cm gives \(A=\frac12(10)(6)=30\) cm². A parallelogram with the same base and height has area 60 cm².

items.title: Trapezium
items.content: Worked example: parallel sides 8 cm and 14 cm, height 5 cm. \(A=\frac12(8+14)5=55\) cm².

items.title: Circle
items.content: Use radius, not diameter, in \(A=\pi r^2\). Worked example: diameter 14 cm gives \(r=7\) cm, so \(C=44\) cm and \(A=154\) cm² using \(\pi=22/7\).

items.title: Composite and shaded figures
items.content: Add non-overlapping component areas, or subtract a hole from the outer area. Worked example: a 10 cm square with a 4 cm square cut out has shaded area \(100-16=84\) cm².

items.title: Reverse dimensions and practical cost
items.content: Work backward from the area formula. Worked example: a rectangle has area 96 m² and length 12 m, so breadth is \(96/12=8\) m. Fencing cost uses perimeter; flooring cost uses area.

items.title: Rhombus, kite and circular parts
items.content: A rhombus or kite can be split into right triangles by its diagonals. Worked example: diagonals 10 cm and 8 cm give area ( rac12(10)(8)=40) cm². A 90° sector of radius 4 cm has area ( rac{90}{360}pi(16)=4pi) cm².

items.title: Find perimeter or area from dimensions
items.content: Worked example: a 9 m by 4 m floor needs \(9\times4=36\) m² of covering. Use the area, not perimeter.

items.title: Find a missing dimension
items.content: Worked example: a triangle has area 42 cm² and base 12 cm. From \(A=bh/2\), \(h=2A/b=84/12=7\) cm.

items.title: Composite or cut-out region
items.content: Worked example: a 14 cm by 10 cm rectangle contains a 4 cm by 3 cm hole. Remaining area is \(140-12=128\) cm².

items.title: Boundary and cost word problem
items.content: Worked example: fencing a 20 m by 15 m field needs \(2(20+15)=70\) m. At ₹40 per metre, cost is ₹2,800.

items.title: Compare shapes
items.content: For equal perimeters, compare areas using each shape’s formula; for a boundary task, do not compare area. Worked example: a 6 cm square has area 36 cm²; a 9 cm by 3 cm rectangle with the same perimeter 24 cm has area 27 cm².

items.title: Diagonal or sector-area question
items.content: Use perpendicular diagonals for a rhombus/kite or the angle fraction of a full circle for a sector. Worked example: a kite with diagonals 12 cm and 7 cm has area ( rac12(12)(7)=42) cm².

items.title: Triangle area
items.content: A triangle is half of a parallelogram with the same base and perpendicular height. Therefore \(A=bh/2\).

items.title: Parallelogram area
items.content: Cut the right triangle at one end and translate it to the other end. The shape becomes a rectangle of base \(b\) and height \(h\), so its area is \(bh\).

items.title: Trapezium area
items.content: Join two congruent trapeziums to form a parallelogram with base \(a+b\) and height \(h\). The pair has area \((a+b)h\), so one trapezium has \(\frac12(a+b)h\).

items.title: Circle area by sector rearrangement
items.content: Divide the circle into many narrow sectors and alternate them. The arrangement approaches a rectangle with height \(r\) and base half the circumference, \(\pi r\). Thus \(A=\pi r^2\).

items.title: Derive rhombus and kite area
items.content: The diagonals split the figure into four right triangles. Their total area is ( rac12d_1d_2), since the four triangles together use half the product of the diagonal lengths.

sections.title: Common errors and how to avoid them

items.title: Confusing perimeter and area
items.content: Perimeter is a length; area is square units. Choose the measure that matches the task: fencing uses boundary, carpet uses surface.

items.title: Using slant height as triangle height
items.content: Triangle height must meet the base at a right angle.

items.title: Using diameter as radius
items.content: If the diameter is given, halve it before using \(\pi r^2\).

items.title: Adding composite boundaries incorrectly
items.content: For an internal cut-out, subtract area. Do not include internal edges in the outside perimeter unless asked for the exposed boundary.

items.title: Using a non-perpendicular height or diagonal
items.content: Use the perpendicular height for base-height formulas and perpendicular diagonals for the rhombus/kite formula.

keyTakeaways: Area is measured in square units and perimeter in linear units.
Triangle and trapezium formulas contain a factor of one half.
Circle formulas use radius; circumference can use diameter.
Composite area is found by addition or subtraction of simple areas.

questionTypes: Find perimeter or area from dimensions
